prompt.context: Our client is the Alaskan business unit of a large multi-national oil & gas company that is drilling on the north shore of Alaska. Due to its isolated location the company has to provide all necessities for its employees including food, housing, utilities, transport, etc.
prompt.question: Recently the company has been facing higher diesel fuel costs. How can we help?

clarifying_info.q: What is diesel used for at the facility?
clarifying_info.a: There is no other source of fuel. The machinery, utilities, transportation, and housing all use diesel.

clarifying_info.q: Is this company making diesel or is this a cost?
clarifying_info.a: The company is drilling crude oil but does not currently refine the oil into diesel.

clarifying_info.q: Is there a reason why costs have increased?
clarifying_info.a: The EPA has recently required cleaner fuel which requires increased refining resulting in higher diesel prices.

clarifying_info.q: How are we currently sourcing our diesel?
clarifying_info.a: We are currently buying our fuel in Anchorage and paying to ship it 500 miles to the North Shore facility.

framework: Internal — Reduce fuel usage: Transportation (reduce frequency/increase utilization of shipments, change transport method to most fuel-efficient option); Operations (improve fuel efficiency of drilling machinery, reduce onsite utility/electricity consumption)
Internal — Reduce purchase price: Vertical integration / reduce third-party dependencies (e.g., build own refinery); Oil futures hedging; Find a closer fuel source; Lobbying for subsidies
External — Assess whether this is company-specific or industry-wide: Competitors' cost structures; Long-term diesel price trends; Macro market trends

questions.prompt: How could we figure out our client's competitors' diesel costs?
questions.guidance: Strong answers cover both direct methods (review public financial reports for cost structure, contact competitor directly) and indirect methods (call sourcing/supply companies for market data, back into prices using competitor location and cost structure, purchase benchmarking data from third-party providers). Interviewer should push with 'what else' until the candidate exhausts the list.

questions.prompt: The client is considering building their own refinery at the North Shore to eliminate third-party transportation costs. Should they build it? The company has a 5-year breakeven requirement. Evaluate this decision.
questions.guidance: Candidate should structure a breakeven analysis. Key data to elicit or use: capital expenditure $150M; current total cost per gallon = $4.00 (purchase) + $0.50 (transport) + $0.75 (storage) = $5.25/gal; post-refinery cost per gallon = $3.40 (drill+refine) + $0.75 (storage) = $4.15/gal (storage costs remain both before and after); annual volume = 26,000,000 gallons. Incremental saving = $1.10/gal; annual savings = $28.6M; 5-year savings = $143M vs. $150M capex — falls 5% short. Candidate must then drive to insights and sensitivity discussion.

math.setup: Compare total all-in cost per gallon before vs. after building the refinery, multiply by annual volume, then compare 5-year cumulative savings to $150M capex.
steps: Post-refinery cost/gal: $3.40 (drill & refine) + $0.75 (storage) = $4.15/gal  [note: storage persists; transportation cost eliminated]
Compare to capex: $143M < $150M — project misses 5-year breakeven by ~$7M (~5%)
math.answer: 5-year cumulative savings of $143M fall ~5% short of the $150M capital expenditure; the project narrowly misses the client's breakeven threshold.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the pros and cons of building the refinery?

categories.name: Pros
ideas: Diesel prices may rise in the future, increasing savings beyond the model
Refinery may have more than 5 years of useful life, improving long-term ROI
Client could sell excess diesel to other companies or projects drilling in the region, increasing annual contribution

categories.name: Cons
ideas: Diesel prices could drop, reducing the value of cost savings
Building the refinery could increase on-site diesel consumption, eroding savings
There may be lower-risk cost-reduction alternatives (e.g., reducing consumption) that achieve similar savings without capex
The client may lack the core competency or capability to operate a refinery

recommendation: Go: The client should begin construction on the new refinery. The project falls only ~5% short of the 5-year breakeven threshold, and rising diesel prices driven by EPA regulations are likely to increase savings over time. Assuming the client has the competency to operate a refinery, the long-term benefits outweigh near-term costs.

No-Go: The client should not build the refinery. The project misses the 5-year breakeven by ~5%, and construction budgets are typically underestimated, likely pushing the payback period further out. The operation is outside the client's core competency and carries significant execution risk. The initial framework identified other cost-reduction strategies (consumption reduction, logistics optimization) that offer meaningful savings with far lower risk.
risks: Construction cost overruns are common — the $150M estimate may be understated, worsening the breakeven gap
Diesel price movements in either direction materially change the NPV
Operating a refinery may be outside the client's core competency
EPA or other regulatory changes could affect refinery operations
Increased on-site diesel availability could lead to higher consumption, eroding savings
next_steps: Validate the $150M construction cost estimate with independent engineering assessment
Model sensitivity of breakeven to diesel price scenarios (+/- 10–20%)
Quantify cost savings from alternative strategies (logistics optimization, fuel efficiency improvements) to compare against refinery option
Assess client's organizational capability to manage a refinery operation
Explore whether diesel could be sold to third parties to improve the investment case
